_meta.note: Pre-check and post-check are parallel items (same objectives, different situations). Objectives are numbered as in design/learning-objectives.md.

preCheck.prompt: A student writes 2(x − 4) = 2x − 4. Which response keeps the student doing the thinking?

options.why: A question at the spot where the error is lets the student find the fix (probing question, P3).
Naming the misconception gives the diagnosis away; the student has nothing left to figure out.
Correcting it makes the line right, but the student produced nothing.

preCheck.prompt: After you ask the group a question, how long should you wait before speaking again?

options.why: About a second was the typical wait in Rowe's classroom studies. At that pace the fastest student answers for everyone.
Waiting 3–5 seconds gives quieter students time to answer (wait time, Q4).

options.text: Until the first hand goes up
options.why: The first hand up is usually the same student every time; others stop trying.

preCheck.prompt: Three minutes are left and the exit ticket hasn't been given. A student asks a great question about a harder problem. What do you do?

options.text: Answer the question and skip the ticket today.
options.why: Skipping the exit ticket breaks the data loop; next session's review has nothing to go on.

options.text: Park the question for next session and give the exit ticket.
options.why: Protecting the ticket keeps the data loop intact, and the question becomes next session's opener (S3, D1).

options.text: Squeeze in the harder problem, then a quick ticket.
options.why: A rushed ticket gives weak data. A good instinct at the wrong time.

postCheck.prompt: A student turns 3x − 5 = 10 into 3x = 5. What's the strongest first response?

options.text: "Check the −5. What happens to it when it moves?"
options.why: It points at the spot without naming the error, so the student does the repair.
A partial step jumps up the hint ladder before the student has looked again.
Naming the label hands over the diagnosis.

postCheck.prompt: While you explain, a student stops writing and looks toward the window. What does that most likely tell you?

options.why: Possible, but a pencil down and eyes away while you're explaining usually means the opposite.

options.text: They may be confused or checked out. Ask them a question.
options.why: Body language is the earliest signal. A direct, low-stakes question brings them back in.
Waiting for a wrong answer means you notice too late.

postCheck.prompt: A discouraged student has failed the same step three times. What's the best move?

options.text: Give one more hint on the same step.
options.why: After three failures, more hints turn struggle unproductive (P7).

options.text: Acknowledge it, work a similar problem all the way through, then return to theirs.
options.why: A worked example after repeated failure consolidates the step (P7, Q5).

options.text: Show the full solution so they can move on.
options.why: The full solution is a last resort after a worked example; here it confirms 'I can't do it'.

reflection.prompt: Pick one moment from the timeline. What would you do differently, and what cue would tell you it was working?
You'll see a real group next week. Which one move will you practice first, and how will you know you did it?

rubricLevels.1: absent, or the failure mode dominates
rubricLevels.4: consistent, specific, and the student does the thinking
